clue.text: Vigour of the Steel debate

parts.note: the swordsman's strokes with the edge and the point of a blade stand for a vigorous, lively exchange of argument

explanation.surface: A heated argument in a steelworks town, or about the steel industry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steel' looks like the industry, but here it is a sword: a debate fought with steel is swordplay, slashing and stabbing, and the phrase for those strokes also means lively argument.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the slashing and stabbing of swordplay and, by extension, any vigorous back-and-forth argument.

clue.text: Wind-machine

parts.note: wind is read as the verb rhyming with 'find', to coil rope around a drum, not the moving air

explanation.definitionFit: A ship's revolving drum used to haul in cable and hoist anchor is a machine for winding.

clue.text: A drop of "the cratur in the city

indicators.note: a drop is a small portion of the liquor, so only part of the run of letters is taken

explanation.surface: An Irishman takes a drop of whiskey, 'the cratur', somewhere in town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The cratur' is Irish slang for whiskey, so 'a drop of' reads as a dram; it actually takes a small slice of the letters across 'cratur in'.
explanation.definitionFit: The northern Italian capital of Piedmont is a major city.

clue.text: They're annoying, when one's among the shades

indicators.note: one piece sits among the letters of another, so it goes inside

parts.note: shades of colour or meaning are subtle nuances
one gives I, and the 's is read as 'is', the S

explanation.surface: Something irritating happens when a person wanders among ghosts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shades' suggests ghosts or shadows, but it means subtle differences; I'S (one's) goes into those to make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pests and irritants are things or people that annoy, which is what this plural noun describes.

clue.text: Flipping bad luck for the rider

definitions.meaning: flipping a coin into the air to decide something
a horseman's fall, being thrown from the saddle

explanation.definitionFit: The word means throwing a coin up to decide, and also a heavy fall from a horse, unlucky for its rider.

clue.text: Surtees's plain alternative

parts.note: R. S. Surtees wrote a novel called 'Plain or ...?', and this is the alternative to 'plain' in that title

explanation.surface: A Victorian sporting novelist offers a simpler choice.
explanation.walkthrough: R. S. Surtees was a Victorian comic novelist of fox-hunting life; one of his books is titled 'Plain or Ringlets?', so the alternative to plain hair is curls.
explanation.definitionFit: The title offers a choice between straight hair and long curled locks, the other option to plain.

clue.text: Evelyn Wood

parts.note: John Evelyn's 1664 treatise on forest trees bore the Latin word for a wood as its title

explanation.walkthrough: The two words read as the name of the Victorian field marshal Sir Evelyn Wood, but they mean the diarist John Evelyn's book on woodland.
explanation.definitionFit: John Evelyn's famous book on forestry took its title from the Latin word for a wood or forest.

clue.text: Judge of beauty, he's more than one bound to get beaten

definitions.text: more than one bound to get beaten

parts.note: in Greek myth Paris judged which goddess was most beautiful
taken as written, the letters of 'he's'

explanation.surface: A beauty-contest judge feels compelled to lose to more than one rival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' looks like 'certain', but it is a noun: in the English custom of beating the bounds, people walk a parish boundary striking its markers.
explanation.definitionFit: Church districts have boundaries ceremonially beaten in the old English custom of beating the bounds.

clue.text: The last man to try to argue with Hobson

definitions.text: The last man to try to argue with Hobson

parts.words: The last man to try to argue with Hobson
parts.note: Hobson's choice is no choice at all, and the proverb says a person in need cannot be a chooser

explanation.surface: Nobody would dare dispute anything with a man called Hobson.
explanation.walkthrough: Hobson's choice means taking what is offered or nothing; the proverb 'they can't be choosers' is said of a penniless person, the least likely to quarrel with that offer.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says a destitute person cannot be choosy, so would never dispute a take-it-or-leave-it offer.

clue.text: Treacly biscuits still available for a man of law

parts.note: parkin is a sticky oatmeal and treacle cake from northern England, here plural
something still on is still available, as on a menu

explanation.surface: Sticky biscuits remain on offer for a lawyer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A man of law' suggests a lawyer, but it is the author of Parkinson's Law, that work expands to fill the time available. Parkin is a ginger and treacle cake from Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: C. Northcote Parkinson gave his name to a famous law about work filling the time allotted.

clue.text: Summer's is short-dated said the bard

definitions.text: Summer's is short-dated said the bard

parts.words: Summer's is short-dated said the bard
parts.note: Shakespeare's Sonnet 18 says summer's ... hath all too short a date

explanation.surface: Shakespeare remarks that the summer passes too quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is from Shakespeare's Sonnet 18: 'And summer's lease hath all too short a date'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare pictures summer as a rented term that runs out too soon, a tenancy agreement with a short date.

clue.text: Felled by Long Melford, the flaming robot !

definitions.text: Felled by Long Melford, the flaming robot !

parts.words: Felled by Long Melford, the flaming robot
parts.note: in Borrow's novel Lavengro the Flaming ... is knocked down by the punch called Long Melford, and the Wizard of Oz has a metal robot man

explanation.surface: A burning robot is knocked over in a Suffolk village.
explanation.walkthrough: Long Melford is a Suffolk village, but in George Borrow's Lavengro it is the hero's long right-hand blow that floors the brutal Flaming Tinman; the Tin Man of Oz supplies the robot.
explanation.definitionFit: Borrow's Flaming Tinman is a tinker felled in a fight, and the Wizard of Oz's metal man is a robot figure.

clue.text: A gang moil till they disperse in the dusk

indicators.note: a gang that disperses scatters, so these letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A gang toils until its members go home at nightfall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A gang moil' sounds like workers toiling; the letters of GANG MOIL scatter, as signalled by 'disperse', into the Scots word for twilight.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scots and poetic word for twilight names the dim light of evening.

clue.text: It's nice to turn in, did you remark ?

indicators.note: turning the letters around means rearranging them

explanation.surface: Someone observes that going to bed early is pleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn in' reads as going to bed; 'turn' tells you to rearrange NICE TO, and 'remark' is used in its sense of observe.
explanation.definitionFit: To remark something in the old sense is to observe or perceive it.

clue.text: Nationally could have, painful associations as touching the kilted.

definitions.text: Nationally could have, painful associations as touching the kilted.

parts.words: Nationally could have, painful associations as touching the kilted
parts.note: a prickly plant that is the national emblem of Scotland would hurt bare knees beneath a kilt

explanation.surface: A national symbol might prove painful for a Highlander in a kilt.
explanation.walkthrough: The prickly plant is Scotland's national emblem, and a kilt leaves the legs bare to its spines.
explanation.definitionFit: The spiny weed that serves as Scotland's emblem would sting a kilt-wearer's bare legs.

clue.text: Susie mending shirt, etc

indicators.note: mending things puts them right, so the letters are reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: A woman repairs a shirt and other clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: The music-hall song 'Sister Susie's Sewing Shirts for Soldiers' makes Susie a seamstress.
explanation.definitionFit: Susie of the wartime song sews shirts, so she is someone who sews.

clue.text: Little bird at the window asking for his breakfast, Simon ?

parts.words: at the window asking for his breakfast
parts.note: a bird pecking at the glass for food is a knocker, one who taps
the tit is a small songbird

explanation.surface: A small bird pecks at the glass wanting food.
explanation.walkthrough: Simon Tappertit is the conceited apprentice in Dickens's Barnaby Rudge; the bird scene builds his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's Barnaby Rudge features Simon, a locksmith's vain apprentice bearing this surname.

clue.text: Sound fellow takes a bit of a break, being fragile

indicators.note: the word is put to the ear, so a spoken name gives letters that are pronounced the same

parts.note: a fellow is a man, here given the name Jim
a crack is a small break, a fracture

explanation.surface: A healthy man gets a small fracture and becomes delicate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound fellow' looks like a reliable man, but 'Sound' signals that JIM is heard, spelt GIM; 'takes' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Showy but flimsy, the adjective describes cheap, flimsy ornaments that break easily.

clue.text: A blow for Jack here, if public water supplies go wrong

parts.note: water mains carry the public supply
to ail is to be unwell, to go wrong in health

explanation.surface: A setback for a plumber if the town's water supply breaks down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A blow' looks like a setback; it is wind blowing on canvas, and Jack is Jack Tar, a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: The principal sail on a ship is where the wind blows for a seaman.

clue.text: Junketer, if not a tarantella-dancer ?

parts.note: the nursery-rhyme girl ate curds and whey, a junket-like dish, and was frightened by a spider; the tarantella was danced to cure a tarantula bite

explanation.surface: Someone at a feast who might otherwise be dancing an Italian folk dance.
explanation.walkthrough: Little Miss Muffet eats curds and whey (junket) until a spider, the tarantula of the tarantella, frightens her away; the tarantella was said to cure that spider's bite.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyme's little girl eats curds and whey, a dessert like junket, so she is one who eats junket.

clue.text: Resorts to handwriting by fits

parts.note: spa towns are health resorts
MS is the abbreviation for manuscript, writing by hand

explanation.surface: Someone at a holiday town falls back on writing letters by hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resorts to' looks like 'falls back on', but 'Resorts' is a noun, the spa towns.
explanation.definitionFit: Sudden convulsive episodes are seizures or fits.

clue.text: Penny among the soaks in the "Adam and Eve " ?

indicators.note: one piece sits among the letters of another, so it goes inside

parts.note: souses are drunkards, as soaks are

explanation.surface: A coin dropped among the drunks in a pub called the Adam and Eve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Adam and Eve' reads as a pub name full of soaks, but the pair are the first married couple.
explanation.definitionFit: The first man and woman were husband and wife, a married couple.

clue.text: Plumped-up cravat for Mr Bull ?

parts.note: plumped up means fattened, fat
a stock is a wide band of cloth worn round the neck

explanation.surface: John Bull wears a well-padded neckcloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mr Bull' suggests John Bull, the figure for England; here he is a farm bull fattened for market.
explanation.definitionFit: Cattle fed up for slaughter are livestock fattened for market, which a bull may be.

clue.text: It's an advantage to put up folding seats, girl

indicators.note: in a down entry putting a word up writes it from the bottom, so it reads backwards

parts.note: an asset is a benefit or advantage

explanation.surface: Folding chairs are handy to set out, says a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: ASSET turned upward gives the name; 'folding seats' is a second route, an anagram of SEATS, also making it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tessa is a female first name, so stands for a girl.

clue.text: Shepherdess put about by child's play

indicators.note: putting a ship about turns it round, so the front of the name is swung to the end

parts.note: the nursery-rhyme shepherdess who lost her sheep is Little Bo-Peep

explanation.surface: A shepherdess is upset by a child's game.
explanation.walkthrough: BO-PEEP is cycled by 'put about': BO goes from front to back.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery game of hiding the face and popping out is a game babies play.

clue.text: Low-lying delta in part of S America

indicators.note: one piece goes in another, inside its letters

parts.note: Peru is a country forming part of South America
Delta is the radio code word for D

explanation.surface: Flat land at a river mouth in a South American country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low-lying delta' looks like a river mouth, but 'Low-lying' means hiding, lying low.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-derived word describes someone hidden or lying in wait, keeping out of sight.

clue.text: Coldest composer

parts.note: the Viennese composer Alban shares his surname with a floating mass of ice, the coldest of all

explanation.definitionFit: Alban Berg was an Austrian composer, and the word also means a floating ice mountain.

clue.text: Jug-jug

parts.note: read not as the nightingale's song but as one jug and another, more than one pitcher

explanation.definitionFit: Large water jugs, more than one, are pitchers, so two jugs are a pair of them.

clue.text: Net contributions not substantial

parts.note: a net is made of holes as much as cord, and those holes are its insubstantial parts

explanation.surface: After deductions, the amounts paid in were small.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Net contributions' looks like money after tax, but a net is a fishing net, and its holes add nothing solid.
explanation.definitionFit: Openings or gaps are empty spaces, contributing nothing solid to a mesh.

clue.text: Holidays that leave you quite done-up ?

definitions.text: Holidays that leave you quite done-up ?

parts.words: Holidays that leave you quite done-up
parts.note: done up reads as exhausted and also as wrapped like a parcel, so the trips are arranged as a parcel deal

explanation.surface: Trips that leave travellers exhausted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Done-up' means worn out, but also tied up like a parcel, which these all-inclusive holidays are.
explanation.definitionFit: All-inclusive trips sold as one bundle of travel and hotel are holidays wrapped as a parcel.
